title: Flow of control in a call
blurb: Control jumps into the function, parameters get bound, the body runs, and the return value flows back.

notes.1: def only creates the function and binds the name volume. The body does NOT run yet.
notes.4: The call: control jumps into volume and the formal parameters length, breadth, height are bound to the actual parameters 10, 5, 3.
notes.2: Inside the function: vol = 10 * 5 * 3 = 150, stored in the function's own local scope.
notes.3: return hands 150 back and control returns to line 4, where it is assigned to v.
notes.5: print shows the value that was returned.

title: Mutation vs rebinding
blurb: The parameter is a new name for the same object: rebinding an int is invisible to the caller, mutating a list is not.

notes.1: Defines modify.
notes.4: x refers to the int 10.
notes.5: L refers to a list object.
notes.6: Call: n and lst become extra names for the SAME objects as x and L - lst points to the same list as L.
notes.2: n + 1 creates a NEW int 11 and rebinds the local name n. The caller's x is untouched.
notes.3: append changes the one shared list object in place, so the caller's L sees it too.
notes.7: x is still 10, but L now contains 99.

title: Positional vs keyword binding
blurb: See how each call binds its values to length, breadth and height - and why a duplicate value fails.

notes.1: Defines volume with three parameters.
notes.3: Positional: values are matched by ORDER - length=10, breadth=5, height=3.
notes.4: Same function, different order: length=5, breadth=10. The product is the same but the assignment changed.
notes.5: Keyword: values are matched by NAME, so the order of the arguments does not matter.
notes.6: Mixed: positional first (length, breadth), then the keyword height=3.
notes.7: The first positional value 5 already fills length, and length=3 tries to fill it again - Python refuses.
notes.2: The body multiplies the three bound values and returns the product.

title: Mutable default argument
blurb: The default list is created ONCE at def time and shared by every call that omits the argument.

notes.1: The default [] is evaluated right now, once, and stored on the function object.
notes.4: __defaults__ is a tuple that holds the one shared default list.
notes.5: No list supplied, so my_list is bound to the shared default list.
notes.2: append changes the shared list in place.
notes.3: The same list object is returned - r1 now has a second name for it.
notes.6: Again no list supplied: the SAME shared list is reused, it is not fresh.
notes.7: The caller passed [4], so the default is not used. A separate list is appended to.
notes.8: No list supplied again: back to the shared list, which still remembers 1 and 2.
notes.9: r1, r2 and r4 are all the same shared list. r3 is the caller's own list.

title: The None-sentinel fix
blurb: Use None as the default and create the list INSIDE the function so every call starts fresh.

notes.1: The default is the immutable None, so nothing mutable is shared.
notes.6: No list supplied: my_list is None.
notes.2: my_list is None, so the if-branch runs.
notes.3: A brand-new empty list is created for THIS call only.
notes.4: append fills the fresh list.
notes.5: Returns the fresh list.
notes.7: Second call, again None: another brand-new list is created, so it does not remember the first call.
notes.8: The caller passed [4], so my_list is not None and the if-branch is skipped.

title: Positional-only (/) in action
blurb: Parameters before / cannot be passed by keyword.

notes.1: a is positional-only (before /), b is positional-or-keyword, c is keyword-only (after *).
notes.3: a=5 by position, b=10 by keyword, c=15 by keyword - allowed.
notes.4: b may also be given by position - allowed.
notes.5: a is positional-only, so it cannot be passed as a=5.

title: Keyword-only (*) in action
blurb: Parameters after * cannot be passed by position.

notes.1: Same signature as before.
notes.3: a and b by position, c by keyword - allowed.
notes.4: Only two parameters (a, b) accept positional values, so a third positional value is rejected.

title: Pangram: collecting letters
blurb: Walk the phrase once; keep only letters, lower-cased, in a set so duplicates vanish.

notes.1: An empty set - it will collect each letter once.
notes.2: Take the next character from the phrase.
notes.3: isalpha() is True only for letters. Digits, spaces and symbols are skipped.
notes.4: lower() makes P and p the same letter; add() ignores a letter that is already in the set.
notes.5: The number of distinct letters seen.

title: Maximum of three (branching)
blurb: Follow the nested if/else until a return runs.

notes.1: Defines the function (a, b, c are positional-only).
notes.12: a=5, b=20, c=15 are bound by position.
notes.2: 5 > 20 is False, so the outer else-branch runs.
notes.13: max now names the int 20 (and hides the built-in max()).

title: Simple interest (keyword-only)
blurb: A leading * forces every argument to be named.

notes.1: The bare * means P, R, T are all keyword-only.
notes.3: Keywords bind P=1000, R=5, T=2.
notes.2: (1000 * 5 * 2) / 100 = 100.0 - true division gives a float.
notes.4: Prints the interest.
notes.5: Positional values are not allowed at all, so Python rejects the call.

title: A function is an object
blurb: Functions have attributes (__name__), a type, and can be given a second name without being called.

notes.1: def creates a function OBJECT and binds the name add to it. The body does not run yet.
notes.3: print is a function too, so it has attributes. print.__name__ is the string 'print'.
notes.4: add.__name__ is 'add': every function object carries its own name.
notes.5: type(add) is <class 'function'>. A function is an ordinary object whose class is function.
notes.6: f = add has NO brackets, so add is not called. The same function object just gets a second name, f.
notes.7: f is add is True: both names refer to one function object (no copy was made).
notes.8: f(2, 3) calls the function object through its second name. Control jumps into add.
notes.2: The body runs: 2 + 3 = 5 is returned to the caller.
notes.9: print shows the value that was returned.

title: Function as a parameter
blurb: airthmatic receives a function in its parameter f and calls it. Pass sub and f(x, y) means sub(x, y).

notes.1: Defines add. It is not passed anywhere in this run.
notes.3: Defines sub.
notes.5: Defines airthmatic. Its first parameter f is going to receive a function.
notes.7: The call airthmatic(sub, 5, 6): f is bound to the function object sub (no brackets after sub, so it is NOT called), x=5, y=6.
notes.6: f(x, y) calls whatever f refers to. Here f is sub, so control jumps into sub(5, 6).
notes.4: sub computes 5 - 6 = -1 and returns it. airthmatic passes the same value on to its caller.
notes.8: sum holds -1. (Naming a variable sum hides Python's built-in sum().)

title: Function as a return value
blurb: A function can hand back another function. The returned function is then called like any other.

notes.1: Defines fun_airthmatic: it returns the function it receives.
notes.3: Defines add.
notes.5: The call fun_airthmatic(add): funName is bound to the function object add. add is not called (no brackets).
notes.2: return funName hands the function object back to the caller. Still nothing has called add.
notes.6: g(5, 6): g is the returned function, i.e. add itself, so this calls add with a=5, b=6.
notes.4: add returns 5 + 6 = 11.

title: Returning an inner function
blurb: fun_outer builds fun_inner and returns it WITHOUT calling it. Nothing inside fun_inner runs until fun() is called.

notes.1: Defines fun_outer. Nothing inside it runs yet.
notes.6: Calls fun_outer(). Control jumps into its body.
notes.2: print('Outer') runs because fun_outer is running.
notes.3: def fun_inner creates the inner function object. Its body (print 'inner') is NOT run.
notes.5: return fun_inner (no brackets) hands the function object back without calling it. fun_outer's frame is then gone.
notes.7: Prints 'calling inner'. fun_inner has still not run.
notes.8: fun() calls the returned function. Control jumps into fun_inner.
notes.4: Only now does print('inner') run.

title: Inner function (totalArea)
blurb: area exists only while totalArea runs. The three calls were put on separate lines so each one can be seen.

notes.1: Defines totalArea.
notes.2: Running this def creates area INSIDE this call of totalArea. The name area exists only in this frame.
notes.5: area(l, b) calls the inner function with 5 and 10. A new frame is stacked on top of totalArea.
notes.6: Second call, area(b, h) = area(10, 2). a1 = 50 is already stored in totalArea.
notes.3: a = l * b: the product of this call's two arguments, stored in area's own local a.
notes.4: return a sends the product back to totalArea. The area frame disappears.
notes.11: area was created inside totalArea and is local to it. At the top level the name area does not exist.

title: Closure remembers msg and name
blurb: fun_inner is returned after fun_outer has finished, yet it still knows msg and name. The global msg is never used.

notes.1: A global msg = 'hello'. The closure below will NOT use it.
notes.2: Defines fun_outer.
notes.9: Call fun_outer('Chinku'): the parameter name is bound to 'Chinku'.
notes.3: msg = 'Welcome' creates a LOCAL msg inside fun_outer. It shadows the global msg.
notes.4: def fun_inner creates the inner function. It uses msg and name, so Python keeps both alive in cells attached to the function (see the “carries” line).
notes.8: fun_inner is returned and fun_outer finishes. The returned function still carries msg='Welcome' and name='Chinku'. That is a closure.
notes.10: f() calls the returned function. fun_outer is long gone, yet its variables are still available.
notes.5: Prints a line of 10 stars.
notes.6: The f-string uses msg='Welcome' and name='Chinku' from the closure (not the global msg 'hello').
notes.7: Prints the closing line of stars.

title: Closure counter with nonlocal
blurb: Each call of fun_get_counter creates its own count. nonlocal lets the inner function change it. (One call per line.)

notes.1: Defines fun_get_counter.
notes.8: First call: creates a private counter for c1.
notes.2#1: count = 0 is this call's own variable.
notes.3#1: Creates the inner function. It changes count, so count is kept in a cell attached to the function. (nonlocal is only a declaration, so it is not a step of its own.)
notes.7#1: Returns the inner function. count (0) travels with it.
notes.9: Second call: creates a completely separate counter for c2.
notes.2#2: A brand-new count = 0, a different variable from c1's.
notes.3#2: A second, separate inner function object.
notes.7#2: Returns it. c2 now has its own count.
notes.10: c1() runs the inner function. nonlocal count means: use fun_get_counter's count, do not create a new local one.
notes.5#1: count += 1 updates the count stored in the closure: 0 becomes 1.
notes.5#2: The closure remembered 1, so it becomes 2.
notes.5#3: The closure remembered 2, so it becomes 3.
notes.5#4: c2 has its own count (0), so it becomes 1. c1 and c2 do not share.
notes.6: return count sends the new value back to the caller.

title: Counter without nonlocal
blurb: Extra: the same counter without nonlocal. count += 1 makes count a local name, so reading it first fails.

notes.1: Defines fun_get_counter.
notes.2: count = 0 inside fun_get_counter.
notes.3: Creates the inner function. It has no nonlocal declaration this time.
notes.4: count is ASSIGNED in this function (count += 1), so Python treats count as a LOCAL variable of fun_increment_counter. That local has no value yet, so reading it fails. Adding nonlocal count makes it refer to the outer count.

title: Lambda vs def
blurb: A lambda is an unnamed one-expression function. double and k do the same job; a lambda can also be called on the spot.

notes.1: Defines double with def.
notes.3: A lambda creates an anonymous function object. k is just a name for it, doing the same job as double.
notes.4: double(3): control jumps into the def function.
notes.2: Returns 3 * 2 = 6.
notes.5: k(3) calls the lambda. Its body x * 2 is the value it returns (a lambda has no return keyword), so b = 6.
notes.6: (lambda x, y: x + y)(5, 6) creates the lambda and calls it at once: c = 11.

title: Lambda with filter and map
blurb: filter keeps the items for which the lambda is True. map replaces each item by the lambda's result.
code: mixed = list(map(lambda x: x if x % 2 == 0 else -x, nums))

notes.1: A list of six numbers.
notes.2: filter calls the lambda on each item and keeps the items for which it returns True: 2, 4, 6. list() collects them into a new list.
notes.3: map calls the lambda on each item and collects the results: every number negated.
notes.4: The lambda holds a conditional expression: even numbers stay, odd numbers become negative.
notes.5: Prints the filtered list.

title: Lambda as a sort key
blurb: sorted(..., key=lambda) sorts by the value the lambda returns for each item instead of by the item itself.
code: by_sum = sorted(data, key=lambda x: x[0] + x[1])

notes.1: Three inner lists of the form [number, number, word].
notes.2: No key: lists are compared item by item, so the first number decides the order: 2, 3, 4.
notes.3: key=lambda x: x[0] + x[1] gives 5, 4 and 6 for the three lists, and sorted orders by those keys: 4, 5, 6.
notes.4: key=lambda x: x[2] sorts by the word: 'Five' < 'Four' < 'Six'.
notes.5: Prints the default order.
notes.6: Prints the order by number sum.

title: Callable class (__call__)
blurb: Day() creates an object; d(2) then runs its __call__ method. The weekday dictionary is shortened to three days.

notes.1#1: The class statement starts. Python will run the class body to build the class.
notes.1#2: First thing inside the class body: the class namespace gets its name and module.
notes.2: def __init__ creates a function stored in the class namespace. It does not run yet.
notes.4: def __call__ adds a second method. Defining __call__ is what makes instances callable.
notes.6: Day() creates a new object and Python runs __init__ on it. Control jumps into __init__.
notes.3: __init__ stores the weekday dictionary on the object as self.days.
notes.7: d(2) looks like a function call. Because the class defines __call__, Python runs d.__call__(2): self is d and dayNo is 2.
notes.5#1: self.days[2] is 'tuesday', [0:3] gives 'tue' and capitalize() gives 'Tue'. This is returned.
notes.9: d(7) runs __call__ again, this time with dayNo = 7.

title: Decorator applied by hand
blurb: fun_outer receives fun_display, wraps it in fun_inner and returns the wrapper. f is the wrapper, not fun_display.

notes.1: Defines the decorator fun_outer. Its parameter is a function.
notes.9: Call fun_outer(fun_display): fun_display_fun is bound to the ORIGINAL function.
notes.2: Creates the wrapper fun_inner. It uses fun_display_fun, so that variable is kept in its closure.
notes.6: Returns the wrapper. f is now the wrapper, and the original fun_display lives inside it.
notes.3: The wrapper prints the first line of stars (extra behaviour BEFORE).
notes.4: The wrapper calls the original function it kept in its closure.
notes.5: The wrapper prints the closing stars (extra behaviour AFTER).

title: Decorating by rebinding the name
blurb: fun_display2 = fun_outer(fun_display2) replaces the name with the wrapper. The wrapper still holds the ORIGINAL function.

notes.1: Defines the decorator fun_outer.
notes.9: Called as declared: fun_display2() just prints Hello2.
notes.10: fun_outer(fun_display2) is called with the original function. The result will REPLACE the name fun_display2.
notes.2: Creates the wrapper fun_inner, which keeps the original in its closure.
notes.6: Returns the wrapper. The name fun_display2 now points to the wrapper. The original function is still alive inside the wrapper.
notes.3: Wrapper: first line of stars.
notes.4: The wrapper calls the original function through its closure. This is not recursion: the wrapper holds the old function.
notes.5: Wrapper: closing stars.

title: Decorator with @
blurb: @fun_outer above a def is shorthand for fun_display3 = fun_outer(fun_display3), done as soon as the def runs.

notes.1: Defines the decorator fun_outer.
notes.7#1: @fun_outer: Python first looks up the decorator.
notes.8#1: Then the def below it creates the plain function fun_display3.
notes.7#2: Now Python calls fun_outer(fun_display3), passing the plain function.
notes.2: Creates the wrapper fun_inner, which keeps the original in its closure.
notes.8#2: The returned wrapper is bound to the name fun_display3. This is exactly fun_display3 = fun_outer(fun_display3), done automatically.
notes.3: Wrapper: first line of stars.
notes.4: The wrapper calls the original function.
notes.5: Wrapper: closing stars.

title: Decorating a function with a parameter
blurb: Extra: fun_inner takes no parameters, so it cannot stand in for a function that does. (7A/7B: *args and **kwargs fix this.)

notes.1: Defines the decorator fun_outer.
notes.6#1: The def creates the plain function greet, which takes one parameter.
notes.2: Creates the wrapper fun_inner. Its parentheses are empty: it accepts no arguments.
notes.4: Returns the wrapper.
notes.6#2: The wrapper is bound to the name greet.
notes.8: greet now refers to fun_inner, which accepts NO arguments, but one was passed. Fix: def fun_inner(*args, **kwargs) and pass them on (see 7A and 7B).
